title: Digits That Divide Their Own Number
statement:
You get a positive integer num that contains no zero digit. Go through its decimal digits and count how many of them divide num evenly.

Count every position: if the same digit appears twice and divides num, it counts twice.

examples.why: 35 is divisible by 5 but not by 3.
1 divides it, and so does 2. The digit 2 appears twice, so it counts twice.

hints: num % 10 gives the last digit, and Math.floor(num / 10) drops it.
Peel digits off a copy of num, so the original value is still there to test divisibility against.
For each peeled digit d, add one when num % d is 0.

explain.intuition:
The only subtlety is that you need two versions of the number at once: one that you take apart digit by digit, and the untouched original that each digit must divide. Work on a copy.

The no-zero guarantee means you never divide by 0. Without it, you would have to skip zero digits explicitly.
steps: While x > 0: take d = x % 10, and if num % d == 0, increment count.
pitfalls: Testing x % d on the shrinking copy instead of num % d.
Counting distinct digits only. In 122 the two 2s both count.
Using x / 10 in JavaScript without flooring, which never reaches 0 cleanly.

solutions.title: Through the string form
solutions.idea: Turn num into a string and test each character as a digit.

solutions.title: Peel digits arithmetically
solutions.idea: Take the last digit with % 10 from a copy, test it against the original, then drop it with integer division.

followups: Allow zero digits and skip them. What else changes?
Count how many numbers in a range [lo, hi] are divisible by every one of their own digits. (Digit DP over the LCM of digits.)
